   377→
   378→### Key Callbacks to Implement
   379→
   380→```cpp
   381→// Command processing
   382→void kn5000_cpanel_device::process_command()
   383→{
   384→    uint8_t cmd = m_cmd_buffer[0];
   385→    uint8_t data = m_cmd_buffer[1];
   386→    uint8_t response[16];
   387→    int resp_len = 0;
   388→
   389→    // Determine packet type from high bits
   390→    bool is_right_panel = (cmd & 0xE0) >= 0x80;  // Bits 7-5 >= 4
   391→
   392→    switch (cmd)
   393→    {
   394→    // Initialization commands
   395→    case 0x1F:  // Init (left panel)
   396→    case 0x1D:
   397→    case 0x1E:
   398→    case 0xDD:  // Setup
   399→        // Acknowledge with sync packet
   400→        response[0] = 0x18 | (is_right_panel ? 0x80 : 0);  // Type 3 = sync
   401→        response[1] = 0x00;
   402→        resp_len = 2;
   403→        break;
   404→
   405→    // Query commands
   406→    case 0x20:  // Query left panel
   407→    case 0xE0:  // Query right panel
   408→        if (data == 0x00) {
   409→            // Ping - respond with sync
   410→            response[0] = 0x18;
   411→            response[1] = 0x00;
   412→            resp_len = 2;
   413→        } else if (data == 0x0B || data == 0x10) {
   414→            // Button state query
   415→            // NOTE: Panel selection is via bit 6, NOT the type field!
   416→            // Bit 6 = 0: right panel, Bit 6 = 1: left panel
   417→            int segment = data & 0x0F;
   418→            response[0] = (is_right_panel ? 0x00 : 0x40) | segment;  // Bit 6 for left panel
   419→            response[1] = get_button_segment(segment + (is_right_panel ? 0 : 16));
   420→            resp_len = 2;
   421→        }
   422→        break;
   423→
   424→    case 0x25:  // Left data command
   425→    case 0xE2:
   426→    case 0xE3:
   427→        // Extended data - respond appropriately
   428→        response[0] = 0x18;  // Sync
   429→        response[1] = data;
   430→        resp_len = 2;
   431→        break;
   432→
   433→    case 0x2B:  // Init state array (left)
   434→    case 0xEB:  // Init state array (right)
   435→        // Send all button segments
   436→        // NOTE: Bit 6 selects panel (0=right, 1=left)
   437→        for (int seg = 0; seg < 16; seg++) {
   438→            response[0] = seg | (is_right_panel ? 0x00 : 0x40);  // Bit 6 for left panel
   439→            response[1] = get_button_segment(seg + (is_right_panel ? 0 : 16));
   440→            send_response(response, 2);
   441→        }
   442→        return;
   443→    }
   444→
   445→    if (resp_len > 0) {
   446→        send_response(response, resp_len);
   447→    }
   448→}
   449→```
   450→
   451→### Button State Reporting Format
   452→
   453→Buttons are organized in 11 segments per panel, with 8 buttons per segment.
   454→
   455→#### Control Panel Right (CPR) Button Mapping
   456→
   457→| Segment | Bit 0 | Bit 1 | Bit 2 | Bit 3 | Bit 4 | Bit 5 | Bit 6 | Bit 7 |
   458→|---------|-------|-------|-------|-------|-------|-------|-------|-------|
   459→| **CPR_SEG0** | - | - | - | - | - | TRANSPOSE - | TRANSPOSE + | - |
   460→| **CPR_SEG1** | ORGAN & ACCORDION | ORCHESTRAL PAD | SYNTH | BASS | DIGITAL DRAWBAR | ACCORDION REGISTER | GM SPECIAL | DRUM KITS |
   461→| **CPR_SEG2** | PIANO | GUITAR | STRINGS & VOCAL | BRASS | FLUTE | SAX & REED | MALLET & ORCH PERC | WORLD PERC |
   462→| **CPR_SEG3** | SUSTAIN | DIGITAL EFFECT | DSP EFFECT | DIGITAL REVERB | ACOUSTIC ILLUSION | - | - | - |
   463→| **CPR_SEG4** | LEFT | RIGHT 2 | RIGHT 1 | ENTERTAINER | CONDUCTOR: LEFT | CONDUCTOR: RIGHT 2 | CONDUCTOR: RIGHT 1 | TECHNI CHORD |
   464→| **CPR_SEG5** | - | - | - | SEQUENCER: PLAY | SEQUENCER: EASY REC | SEQUENCER: MENU | - | - |
   465→| **CPR_SEG6** | PM 1 | PM 2 | PM 3 | PM 4 | PM 5 | PM 6 | PM 7 | PM 8 |
   466→| **CPR_SEG7** | PM: SET | PM: NEXT BANK | PM: BANK VIEW | - | - | - | - | - |
   467→| **CPR_SEG8** | - | - | - | R1/R2 OCTAVE - | R1/R2 OCTAVE + | START/STOP | SYNCHRO & BREAK | TAP TEMPO |
   468→| **CPR_SEG9** | - | - | - | - | - | - | MEMORY A | MEMORY B |
   469→| **CPR_SEG10** | - | - | MENU: SOUND | MENU: CONTROL | MENU: MIDI | MENU: DISK | - | - |
   470→

   472→
   473→| Segment | Bit 0 | Bit 1 | Bit 2 | Bit 3 | Bit 4 | Bit 5 | Bit 6 | Bit 7 |
   474→|---------|-------|-------|-------|-------|-------|-------|-------|-------|
   475→| **CPL_SEG0** | STANDARD ROCK | R & ROLL & BLUES | POP & BALLAD | FUNK & FUSION | SOUL & MODERN DANCE | BIG BAND & SWING | JAZZ COMBO | - |
   476→| **CPL_SEG1** | COMPOSER: MEMORY | COMPOSER: MENU | SOUND ARRANGER: SET | SOUND ARRANGER: ON/OFF | MUSIC STYLIST | FADE IN | FADE OUT | - |
   477→| **CPL_SEG2** | FILL IN 1 | FILL IN 2 | INTRO & ENDING 1 | INTRO & ENDING 2 | - | - | PAGE DOWN | PAGE UP |
   478→| **CPL_SEG3** | DEMO | MSP BANK | MSP MENU | MSP STOP/RECORD | - | - | - | - |
   479→| **CPL_SEG4** | VARIATION 1 | VARIATION 2 | VARIATION 3 | VARIATION 4 | MUSIC STYLE ARRANGER | SPLIT POINT | AUTO PLAY CHORD | - |
   480→| **CPL_SEG5** | MSP 1 | MSP 2 | MSP 3 | MSP 4 | MSP 5 | MSP 6 | - | - |
   481→| **CPL_SEG6** | U.S. TRAD | COUNTRY | LATIN | MARCH & WALTZ | PARTY TIME | SHOWTIME & TRAD DANCE | WORLD | CUSTOM |
   482→| **CPL_SEG7** | RIGHT 5 | RIGHT 4 | DISPLAY HOLD | EXIT | DOWN 7 | UP 7 | DOWN 8 | UP 8 |
   483→| **CPL_SEG8** | RIGHT 3 | RIGHT 2 | RIGHT 1 | - | DOWN 5 | UP 5 | DOWN 6 | UP 6 |
   484→| **CPL_SEG9** | LEFT 5 | LEFT 4 | LEFT 3 | - | DOWN 3 | UP 3 | DOWN 4 | UP 4 |
   485→| **CPL_SEG10** | LEFT 2 | LEFT 1 | HELP | OTHER PARTS/TR | DOWN 1 | UP 1 | DOWN 2 | UP 2 |

   487→**Known button combinations (from firmware):**
   488→
   489→| Segment | Bitmask | Buttons | Effect |
   490→|---------|---------|---------|--------|
   491→| CPL_SEG4 | 0x6C | AUTO PLAY CHORD + SPLIT POINT + VAR4 + VAR3 | Display software build numbers |
   492→| CPR_SEG1 | 0x70 | GM SPECIAL + ACCORDION REGISTER + DIGITAL DRAWBAR | Display firmware version |
   493→| CPL_SEG6 | 0x38 | SHOWTIME & TRAD DANCE + PARTY TIME + MARCH & WALTZ | Unknown function |
   494→| CPR_SEG6 | 0x0F | PM 1 + PM 2 + PM 3 + PM 4 | Firmware update mode |

   496→### LED Control Interface
   497→
   498→LEDs are controlled via the `CPANEL_LED_TX_BUFFER` array (60 bytes at 0x8E01):
   499→
   500→```cpp
   501→void kn5000_cpanel_device::update_leds(int index, uint8_t pattern)
   502→{
   503→    // Index wraps at 0x3C (60)
   504→    index %= 60;
   505→    m_led_state[index] = pattern;
   506→
   507→    // Map LED index to physical LEDs
   508→    // The LED array is transmitted in 2-byte sequences
   509→    // Byte 0: Row select (bits 5-0 = row, bits 7-6 = panel select)
   510→    // Byte 1: Column pattern (which LEDs in row are lit)
   511→
   512→    // Update MAME output for visual feedback
   513→    for (int bit = 0; bit < 8; bit++) {
   514→        machine().output().set_indexed_value("led", index * 8 + bit, BIT(pattern, bit));
   515→    }
   516→}
   517→```
   518→
   519→#### Control Panel Right (CPR) LED Mapping
   520→

   544→### Rotary Encoder Format
   545→
   546→Encoders send signed delta values via Type 2 packets:
   547→
   548→```cpp
   549→void kn5000_cpanel_device::process_encoder(int encoder_id, int8_t delta)
   550→{
   551→    // Known Encoder IDs (from firmware analysis):
   552→    // 2: Data wheel / jog wheel -> ENCODER_0_OUTPUT
   553→    // 5: Volume slider / expression -> ENCODER_1_OUTPUT, MIDI_CC_VOLUME_VALUE
   554→    // Other IDs (0-1, 3-4, 6-31) return 0xFFFF (no handler)
   555→
   556→    m_encoder_delta[encoder_id] += delta;
   557→
   558→    // Report encoder change
   559→    // Byte 0 format: [ ID_hi[1:0] | 0 | 1 | 0 | ID_lo[2:0] ]
   560→    //                  bits 7-6     5   4   3   bits 2-0
   561→    // Type 2 = bits 5-3 = 010 = 0x10
   562→    uint8_t response[2];
   563→    response[0] = 0x10 | (encoder_id & 0x07) | ((encoder_id & 0x18) << 3);  // Type 2 + encoder ID
   564→    response[1] = delta;
   565→    send_response(response, 2);
   566→}
   567→```
   568→
   569→### MIDI Controller Output
   570→
   571→Encoder and analog input values are converted to MIDI Control Change messages and stored in RAM variables before being sent to the sound engine:
   572→
   573→**Controller Mapping:**
   574→
   575→| Variable | MIDI CC# | Controller Name |
   576→|----------|----------|-----------------|
   577→| `MIDI_CC_EXPRESSION_VALUE` | 0 | Bank Select MSB / Expression |
   578→| `MIDI_CC_MODWHEEL_VALUE` | 1 | Modulation Wheel |
   579→| `MIDI_CC_BREATH_VALUE` | 2 | Breath Controller |
   580→| `MIDI_CC_FOOT_VALUE` | 4 | Foot Controller |
   581→| `MIDI_CC_VOLUME_VALUE` | 7 | Volume (estimated) |
   582→
   583→**Change Detection:**
   584→
   585→The `*_PENDING` variants (e.g., `MIDI_CC_MODWHEEL_PENDING`) use bit 7 as a "value changed" flag:
   586→- When an encoder/ADC value changes, bit 7 is set
   587→- The MIDI output routine checks bit 7, sends the value if set, then clears bit 7
   588→- This prevents redundant MIDI messages for unchanged values
   589→
   590→**MIDI Message Format (at 0x9127-0x912A):**
   591→
   592→| Address | Field | Example |
   593→|---------|-------|---------|
   594→| 0x9127 | Status byte | 0xB0 (Control Change, channel 0) |
   595→| 0x9128 | Controller # | 0x01 (Modulation) |
   596→| 0x9129 | Value | 0x00-0x7F |
   597→| 0x912A | Velocity/Range | 0x7F |

   874→## 10. DEMO Button Code Path (Case Study)
   875→
   876→This section traces the complete code path from when a user presses the DEMO button to when the demo mode handler executes.
   877→
   878→### Button Press Detection
   879→
   880→When DEMO is pressed (CPL_SEG3, bit 0):
   881→
   882→```
   883→Hardware interrupt (serial RX)
   884→    ↓
   885→CPanel_RX_ButtonPacket (0xFC4985)
   886→    - Reads segment byte (3) and button state (bit 0)
   887→    - XORs new state with previous to detect change
   888→    - Queues event to CPANEL_RX_EVENT_QUEUE
   889→```
   890→
   891→### Event Queue
   892→
   893→- **Location:** `CPANEL_RX_EVENT_QUEUE` (0x000200AD)
   894→- **Size:** 128 bytes circular buffer
   895→- **Content:** Changed bits mask + segment info
   896→
   897→### Application Event Dispatch
   898→
   899→```
   900→ApDeliveryEvent (0xFA9E09) - Called from main loop
   901→    ↓
   902→LABEL_F44147 (0xF44147) - Event Dispatcher
   903→    - Extracts event code (0x01c00013)
   904→    - Indexes APP_EVENT_HANDLER_TABLE with handler ID
   905→    - Jumps to handler
   906→    ↓
   907→DemoModeFunc (0xF222DD, line 179085)
   908→```
   909→
   910→### Event Code Encoding: `0x01c00013`
   911→
   912→```
   913→01c00013h breakdown:
   914→  0x01   = Button event group identifier
   915→  0xc0   = LEFT panel segment encoding
   916→  0x00   = Padding/flags
   917→  0x13   = Handler index 19 (DEMO button handler)
   918→```
   919→
   920→### DemoModeFunc Handler (0xF222DD)
   921→
   922→```asm
   923→DemoModeFunc:
   924→    CP XBC, 01c00013h        ; Verify this is DEMO button event
   925→    JR NZ, LABEL_F222FA      ; Not DEMO? Exit
   926→    CP XDE, 00000001h        ; Check if button released (XDE=1)
   927→    JR Z, LABEL_F222EE       ; Released → call LABEL_F869E3
   928→    OR XDE, XDE              ; Check if button pressed (XDE=0)
   929→    JR NZ, LABEL_F222FA      ; Neither? Exit
   930→    ; Button pressed (XDE=0) → call LABEL_F8696F
   931→    CALL LABEL_F8696F        ; Demo mode entry routine
   932→```

   946→### Complete Call Chain
   947→
   948→```
   949→Hardware interrupt (serial RX)
   950→    ↓
   951→CPanel_RX_Process
   952→    ↓
   953→CPanel_RX_ParseNext (line 401556)
   954→    ↓
   955→CPanel_RX_ButtonPacket (0xFC4985)

     3→title: "Debugging the Serial Protocol: A Deep Dive"
     4→permalink: /serial-debugging/
     5→---
     6→
     7→# Debugging the KN5000 Serial Communication: A Journey Through Synchronous Serial Timing
     8→
     9→*January 2026*
    10→
    11→This post documents our debugging journey attempting to get the MAME driver's control panel HLE (High Level Emulation) communicating correctly with the emulated TMP94C241 CPU. What started as a simple "serial communication isn't working" bug turned into a deep exploration of synchronous serial timing edge cases.
    12→
    13→## The Problem
    14→
    15→The KN5000 keyboard uses a synchronous serial protocol between the main CPU (TMP94C241) and the control panel MCUs (two Mitsubishi M37471M2196S chips that handle buttons, LEDs, and rotary encoders). Since we don't have ROM dumps for the control panel MCUs, we're using High Level Emulation - our code pretends to be the MCUs by implementing the protocol based on reverse engineering.
    16→
    17→During boot, the keyboard was showing "ERROR in CPU data transmission" - the main CPU couldn't establish communication with the control panel.
    18→
    19→## Understanding the Protocol
    20→
    21→The TMP94C241 CPU uses I/O Interface Mode for serial communication - a synchronous protocol where:
    22→- The CPU is the **master**, generating the clock signal (SCLK)
    23→- The control panel is the **slave**, responding to clock edges
    24→- Data is transmitted LSB-first, 8 bits per byte
    25→- **Rising edge**: Both sides sample incoming data
    26→- **Falling edge**: Both sides output the next bit
    27→
    28→The clock is derived from Timer 2's output compare trigger (TO2), giving us a 31250 Hz baud rate.
    29→
    30→## Issue 1: Clock Not Being Generated
    31→
    32→Our first discovery was that clock pulses weren't reaching the control panel at all. The `TO2_trigger` function was checking the wrong condition:
    33→
    34→```cpp
    35→// WRONG: Checking if IOC bit is SET
    36→if ((m_serial_mode & 3) == 0 && BIT(m_serial_control, 1))
    37→
    38→// CORRECT: IOC=0 means master mode (SCLK output)
    39→if ((m_serial_mode & 3) == 0 && !BIT(m_serial_control, 1))
    40→```
    41→
    42→The IOC bit in the serial control register means:
    43→- **IOC=0**: SCLK is an output (master mode)
    44→- **IOC=1**: SCLK is an input (slave mode)
    45→
    46→The firmware sets `serial_control=0x01` (IOC=0, master mode), but we were checking for IOC=1.
    47→
    48→## Issue 2: Wrong Idle State
    49→
    50→Serial lines idle HIGH, but we had initialized TXD to 0:
    51→
    52→```cpp
    53→// WRONG
    54→m_txd(0)
    55→
    56→// CORRECT
    57→m_txd(1)  // Idle state is HIGH for serial lines
    58→```
    59→
    60→This caused the control panel to receive `0x00` during idle instead of `0xFF`.
    61→
    62→## Issue 3: Byte Boundary Synchronization
    63→
    64→This is where things got interesting. Even with correct clock generation and idle state, the control panel was receiving garbage. The issue: **byte boundaries weren't synchronized**.
    65→
    66→In synchronous serial, both sides need to agree on where each byte starts and ends. The clock runs continuously, so if one side is at bit 3 while the other is at bit 7, they'll never receive correct data.
    67→
    68→### The `tx_start` Callback
    69→
    70→Our first solution was to add a callback from the CPU to the control panel signaling "I'm starting a new byte":
    71→
    72→```cpp
    73→void tmp94c241_serial_device::scNbuf_w(uint8_t data)
    74→{
    75→    m_tx_shift_register = data;
    76→    m_tx_clock_count = 8;
    77→    m_tx_start_cb(1);  // Signal new byte start
    78→    m_txd_cb(m_tx_shift_register & 1);  // Pre-output bit 0
    79→}
    80→```
    81→
    82→The control panel would reset its receive counter when receiving this signal.
    83→
    84→## Issue 4: Bit 0 Output Twice
    85→
    86→After adding byte sync, we noticed the control panel was receiving shifted data. Tracing through the logs revealed that **bit 0 was being output twice**:
    87→
    88→1. `scNbuf_w`: Output bit 0 immediately
    89→2. First falling edge: Output bit 0 again, then shift
    90→
    91→The receiver would sample bit 0 on the first rising edge, then sample bit 0 *again* on the second rising edge (since the falling edge hadn't advanced to bit 1 yet).
    92→
    93→### The Skip-First-Falling Fix
    94→
    95→The solution was to skip the first falling edge after a buffer write:
    96→
    97→```cpp
    98→void tmp94c241_serial_device::scNbuf_w(uint8_t data)
    99→{
   100→    m_tx_shift_register = data;
   101→    m_tx_clock_count = 7;  // 7 more bits after pre-output
   102→    m_txd_cb(m_tx_shift_register & 1);  // Pre-output bit 0
   103→    m_tx_skip_first_falling = true;  // Skip next falling edge
   104→}
   105→```
   106→
   107→But this introduced another bug...
   108→
   109→## Issue 5: Clock Phase Matters
   110→
   111→The skip logic worked when the clock was HIGH at the time of the buffer write, but failed when the clock was LOW:
   112→
   113→**Clock HIGH when writing:**
   114→1. Buffer write: output bit 0
   115→2. Falling edge: skip (bit 0 stays on line)
   116→3. Rising edge: receiver samples bit 0 ✓
   117→4. Falling edge: output bit 1
   118→5. Rising edge: receiver samples bit 1 ✓
   119→
   120→**Clock LOW when writing:**
   121→1. Buffer write: output bit 0
   122→2. Rising edge: receiver samples bit 0 ✓
   123→3. Falling edge: skip (bit 0 stays on line)
   124→4. Rising edge: receiver samples bit 0 AGAIN ✗
   125→
   126→The fix: only skip if the clock is HIGH when writing:
   127→
   128→```cpp
   129→m_tx_skip_first_falling = (m_sioclk_state == 1);
   130→```
   131→
   132→## Issue 6: Repeated Writes During Init
   133→
   134→Even with all timing fixed, the control panel was only receiving `0xFF`. The firmware was in an initialization loop, repeatedly re-writing `0x45` to the serial buffer before a complete byte could be transmitted.
   135→
   136→Each write fired `tx_start`, resetting the control panel's receive counter. The panel would receive 2-3 bits, get reset, receive 2-3 bits, get reset, etc. - never completing a byte.
   137→
   138→### Only Signal on Idle-to-Active Transition
   139→
   140→The solution: only fire `tx_start` when starting a *new* transmission, not when replacing an in-progress byte:
   141→
   142→```cpp
   143→void tmp94c241_serial_device::scNbuf_w(uint8_t data)
   144→{
   145→    bool was_idle = (m_tx_clock_count == 0);
   146→    m_tx_shift_register = data;
   147→    m_tx_clock_count = 7;
   148→
   149→    if (was_idle)
   150→        m_tx_start_cb(1);  // Only signal if we were idle
   151→
   152→    m_txd_cb(m_tx_shift_register & 1);
   153→    m_tx_skip_first_falling = was_idle && (m_sioclk_state == 1);
   154→}
   155→```
   156→
   157→## Current State
   158→
   159→After all these fixes, individual bits are now being transmitted correctly:
   160→- Bit 0 = 1 (shift_reg=0x80) ✓
   161→- Bit 1 = 0 (shift_reg=0x40) ✓
   162→- Bit 2 = 1 (shift_reg=0xA0) ✓
   163→
   164→These match the expected values for `0x45` (binary: 01000101).
   165→
   166→However, the firmware's initialization behavior still prevents complete bytes from being received. The root cause appears to be how the firmware polls/retries during serial setup - it keeps reconfiguring the serial port and rewriting the buffer before transmission completes.
   167→
   168→## Lessons Learned
   169→
   170→1. **Synchronous serial timing is subtle**: The relationship between clock edges, data output, and data sampling must be precisely coordinated.
   171→
   172→2. **Clock phase at write time matters**: The same code can behave differently depending on when in the clock cycle you write data.
   173→
   174→3. **Initialization loops can mask correct behavior**: Even if your protocol implementation is correct, firmware polling/retry behavior during initialization can prevent successful communication.
   175→
   176→4. **Debug logging is essential**: Without detailed logs showing every clock edge, bit output, and bit sample, we never would have traced these timing issues.
   177→
   178→5. **Real hardware has more tolerance**: Physical serial interfaces have electrical characteristics that make them more forgiving of slight timing variations. Emulation requires exact logical correctness.
   179→
   180→## Next Steps
   181→
   182→The remaining challenge is understanding why the firmware keeps re-initializing the serial port during boot. Possibilities include:
   183→
   184→1. The firmware expects a specific response from the control panel that we're not providing
   185→2. There's additional handshaking or status checking we haven't implemented
   186→3. The initialization has specific timing requirements we're not meeting
   187→
   188→We'll continue analyzing the firmware's serial initialization routines to understand exactly what conditions it's checking before proceeding past the init loop.
   189→
   190→## Code References
   191→
   192→The relevant MAME driver files:
   193→- `src/devices/cpu/tlcs900/tmp94c241_serial.cpp` - CPU serial implementation
   194→- `src/mame/matsushita/kn5000_cpanel.cpp` - Control panel HLE
   195→- `src/mame/matsushita/kn5000.cpp` - Main driver
   196→
   197→The firmware serial routines (in the disassembly):
   198→- `CPanel_*` routines handle control panel communication
   199→- Serial initialization happens early in the boot sequence
   200→

## Investigation Summary: SC1MOD Clock Source Configuration

Based on my analysis of the MAME serial implementation, original KN5000 firmware, and your custom ROM configuration, here are my findings regarding whether `LD (SC1MOD), 001h` could fix phantom input issues:

### Current State
Your custom ROM (boot_hw_init.asm, line 129):
```asm
LD (SC1MOD), 000h		; Synchronous I/O mode, clock source = TO2 trigger
```

Original KN5000 firmware (cpanel_routines.asm, line 99):
```asm
LD (SC1MOD), 000h ; serial clk: TO2 trigger
                  ; serial transfer mode: I/O  transfer mode
```

### SC1MOD Register Bits (from MAME implementation)
The SC1MOD register bits 1-0 control the clock source:
- **Value 0x00 (bits 1-0 = 00)**: TO2 trigger clock source
- **Value 0x01 (bits 1-0 = 01)**: Baud rate generator (NOT implemented yet in MAME)
- **Value 0x02 (bits 1-0 = 10)**: Internal clock at φ1 (NOT implemented)
- **Value 0x03 (bits 1-0 = 11)**: External clock on SCLK pin (NOT implemented)

### Key Finding: The Baud Rate Timer ALWAYS Runs
This is the crucial insight: In the MAME serial implementation, the `timer_callback()` function (lines 289-299 of tmp94c241_serial.cpp) **does NOT check the serial_mode bits**. The timer runs independently of whether serial_mode is set for TO2 trigger or baud rate generator mode.

The timer_callback logic:
```cpp
bool need_clock = (m_tx_clock_count > 0) || m_tx_skip_first_falling || (m_rx_clock_count != 8);
if (m_hz && need_clock && (m_cpu->m_port_function[PORT_F] & (1 << (m_channel==0 ? 2: 6))))
{
    sioclk(m_sioclk_state ^ 1);
}
```

This means:
- If `BR1CR` is set (m_hz > 0), the baud rate timer **always** generates clock pulses during TX/RX
- The `serial_mode & 3 == 0` check in `TO2_trigger()` determines if TO2 *also* generates pulses, but the baud timer is independent

### The Real Control: TO2 Trigger Check
The MAME implementation at line 81 shows where serial_mode matters:
```cpp
if ((m_serial_mode & 3) == 0 && !BIT(m_serial_control, 1))
{
    sioclk(state);  // TO2 trigger pulses reach sioclk()
}
```

This means:
- **TO2 trigger mode (serial_mode & 3 == 0)**: TO2 edges trigger clock pulses
- **Baud rate generator mode (serial_mode & 3 == 01)**: TO2 edges are *ignored*, only the BR1CR timer generates pulses

### Answer to Your Questions

1. **Does SC1MOD=0x00 vs 0x01 affect whether the baud rate timer toggles SCLK?**
   - **NO**. The baud rate timer (`timer_callback`) is independent of serial_mode. It always runs and toggles SCLK whenever data is active, regardless of serial_mode setting.

2. **What value does the original firmware use for SC1MOD for the control panel serial?**
   - **0x00** - TO2 trigger mode. The original firmware does NOT use the baud rate generator for control panel communication.

3. **Could SC1MOD=0x00 (TO2 trigger mode) cause the SCLK to be clocked differently than expected?**
   - **Unlikely to be the root cause**. Both TO2 trigger and baud rate generator modes should produce the same frequency clock in MAME (though TO2 would use the TO2 pin interrupt, while baud generator uses its internal timer). The difference is which *source* provides the pulses, not the frequency.

### Potential Issues With SC1MOD=0x01

If you changed to `LD (SC1MOD), 001h` (baud rate generator mode):

**Risk**: The TO2 trigger pulses would be **ignored**. If TO2 is being used elsewhere in the system (e.g., for I/O control timing), it wouldn't function for serial control. However, since BR1CR is set to 0x14 (250 kHz), the baud timer would provide equivalent clocking.

**Benefit**: None identified. The baud rate timer already runs in your current configuration.

### Why Phantom Input Might Occur

The real culprits for phantom input are likely:
1. **Byte boundary desynchronization** - documented in serial-debugging-journey.md as Issue 3-4
2. **Initialization polling behavior** - the firmware keeps reconfiguring serial during boot
3. **Missing CPanel HLE implementation** - your ROM needs the control panel to respond correctly

### Recommendation

**Do NOT change SC1MOD to 0x01**. The original firmware uses 0x00 and that's what the control panel MCUs expect. Changing this would only diverge from the reference implementation without solving phantom input issues.

Instead, focus on:
1. Verifying the control panel HLE is properly responding to serial commands
2. Checking that the TO2 trigger is correctly wired and generating expected pulses
3. Reviewing the MAME serial implementation's handling of TO2_trigger vs. timer_callback interactions

- **Baud rate generator mode (serial_mode & 3 == 01)**: TO2 edges are *ignored*, only the BR1CR timer generates pulses

### Answer to Your Questions

1. **Does SC1MOD=0x00 vs 0x01 affect whether the baud rate timer toggles SCLK?**
   - **NO**. The baud rate timer (`timer_callback`) is independent of serial_mode. It always runs and toggles SCLK whenever data is active, regardless of serial_mode setting.

2. **What value does the original firmware use for SC1MOD for the control panel serial?**
   - **0x00** - TO2 trigger mode. The original firmware does NOT use the baud rate generator for control panel communication.

3. **Could SC1MOD=0x00 (TO2 trigger mode) cause the SCLK to be clocked differently than expected?**
   - **Unlikely to be the root cause**. Both TO2 trigger and baud rate generator modes should produce the same frequency clock in MAME (though TO2 would use the TO2 pin interrupt, while baud generator uses its internal timer). The difference is which *source* provides the pulses, not the frequency.

### Potential Issues With SC1MOD=0x01

If you changed to `LD (SC1MOD), 001h` (baud rate generator mode):

**Risk**: The TO2 trigger pulses would be **ignored**. If TO2 is being used elsewhere in the system (e.g., for I/O control timing), it wouldn't function for serial control. However, since BR1CR is set to 0x14 (250 kHz), the baud timer would provide equivalent clocking.

**Benefit**: None identified. The baud rate timer already runs in your current configuration.

### Why Phantom Input Might Occur

The real culprits for phantom input are likely:
1. **Byte boundary desynchronization** - documented in serial-debugging-journey.md as Issue 3-4
2. **Initialization polling behavior** - the firmware keeps reconfiguring serial during boot
3. **Missing CPanel HLE implementation** - your ROM needs the control panel to respond correctly

### Recommendation

**Do NOT change SC1MOD to 0x01**. The original firmware uses 0x00 and that's what the control panel MCUs expect. Changing this would only diverge from the reference implementation without solving phantom input issues.

Instead, focus on:
1. Verifying the control panel HLE is properly responding to serial commands
2. Checking that the TO2 trigger is correctly wired and generating expected pulses
3. Reviewing the MAME serial implementation's handling of TO2_trigger vs. timer_callback interactions

LD W, 0
	SLA 1, WA
	EXTZ XWA
	LD XIY, VM_VARIABLES
	ADD XIY, XWA
	LD (XIY), DE
	RET


	ifdef TARGET_MAINCPU
; _cpanel_send_byte: Send/receive one byte via SC1 synchronous I/O
; In sync mode, writing SC1BUF simultaneously sends and receives.
; Polls INTRX1 (RX complete) flag in INTES1 to know when the byte
; has been fully clocked in, then reads the received byte from SC1BUF.
; Uses AND instead of BIT (MAME has known flag bugs with DEC; BIT
; might be similarly affected). Includes timeout to prevent hangs.
; Input: A = byte to send
; Output: A = byte received
; Clobbers: A only (DE preserved via stack)
_cpanel_send_byte:
	LD (INTCLR), 022h		; Clear INTRX1 pending (bit 3 of INTES1)
	LD (SC1BUF), A			; Start 8-bit synchronous transfer
	PUSH DE
	LD DE, 0				; Timeout counter (65536 iterations ~57ms at 16MHz)
.wait:
	LD A, (INTES1)			; Read interrupt status
	AND A, 008h				; Test INTRX1 (RX complete) — bit 3
	JR NZ, .done			; Exit when set
	DJNZ DE, .wait			; Decrement timeout, loop if not expired
	; Timeout: serial transfer did not complete
	LDB (DIAG_SERIAL_OK), 055h	; Mark timeout for diagnostic
	POP DE
	LD A, 0					; Return 0 on timeout
	RET
.done:
	LDB (DIAG_SERIAL_OK), 0AAh	; Mark success for diagnostic
	POP DE
	LD A, (SC1BUF)			; Read received byte
	RET

; _cpanel_query_segment: Query a control panel button segment
; Sends 2-byte command, then 2 dummy bytes to clock in response.
; Input: B = command (0x20=left panel, 0xE0=right panel), C = segment number
; Output: A = button bitmap
; Clobbers: A only (B, C preserved)
_cpanel_query_segment:
	LD A, B					; Send command byte
	CALL _cpanel_send_byte
	LD A, C					; Send segment byte
	CALL _cpanel_send_byte
	LD A, 0FFh				; Send dummy (clock in header)
	CALL _cpanel_send_byte	; A = header (discard)
	LD A, 0FFh				; Send dummy (clock in bitmap)
	CALL _cpanel_send_byte	; A = button bitmap
	RET

; _cpanel_init: Initialize control panel serial protocol
; Sends the 5-command init sequence matching the original firmware.
; Each command is followed by a delay. The cpanel MCUs respond with
; sync packets; we consume them via the standard 4-byte exchange.
; Must be called once before any _cpanel_query_segment calls.
; Clobbers: A, B, C, DE
_cpanel_init:
	; Init command 1: 1F DA
	LD B, 01Fh
	LD C, 0DAh
	CALL _cpanel_query_segment
	CALL _cpanel_delay

	; Init command 2: 1F 1A
	LD B, 01Fh
	LD C, 01Ah
	CALL _cpanel_query_segment
	CALL _cpanel_delay

	; Init command 3: 1D 00
	LD B, 01Dh
	LD C, 000h
	CALL _cpanel_query_segment
	CALL _cpanel_delay

	; Init command 4: DD 03
	LD B, 0DDh
	LD C, 003h
	CALL _cpanel_query_segment
	CALL _cpanel_delay

	; Init command 5: 1E 80
	LD B, 01Eh
	LD C, 080h
	CALL _cpanel_query_segment
	CALL _cpanel_delay

	; Clear serial interrupt flags (original firmware uses INTCLR)
	LD (INTCLR), 023h		; Clear INTTX1 pending
	LD (INTCLR), 022h		; Clear INTRX1 pending
	RET

; _cpanel_delay: Inter-command delay for init sequence
; Matches the original firmware's DELAY_3000_LOOPS between init commands.
; Clobbers: DE
_cpanel_delay:
	PUSH DE
	LD DE, 3000h
.loop:
	DJNZ DE, .loop
	POP DE
	RET

	endif ; TARGET_MAINCPU

INPUT_UPDATE_PLAYER:
	ifdef TARGET_MAINCPU

	; Query CPR_SEG4 (right panel segment 4) for direction buttons
	; CPR_SEG4: bit1=UP(PART:RIGHT2), bit4=LEFT(CONDUCTOR:LEFT),
	;           bit5=DOWN(CONDUCTOR:RIGHT2), bit6=RIGHT(CONDUCTOR:RIGHT1)
	LD B, 0E0h				; Right panel command
	LD C, 004h				; Segment 4
	CALL _cpanel_query_segment
	LD H, A					; H = CPR_SEG4 bitmap

	; Query CPL_SEG4 (left panel segment 4) for action button
	; CPL_SEG4: bit3=ACTION(VARIATION 4)
	LD B, 020h				; Left panel command
	; C still = 004h
	CALL _cpanel_query_segment
	LD L, A					; L = CPL_SEG4 bitmap

	; Save raw serial results for VRAM diagnostic
	LD (DIAG_CPR), H
	LD (DIAG_CPL), L

	; DIAGNOSTIC MODE: Write all zeros to input VM variables.
	; Serial results are saved above for the VRAM diagnostic rectangles.
	; If Lester still moves with all-zero input, the bytecode is moving
	; him (scripted animation), not phantom serial data.
	LD DE, 0
	LD A, VM_VARIABLE_HERO_POS_LEFT_RIGHT
	CALL _write_vm_var
	LD DE, 0
	LD A, VM_VARIABLE_HERO_POS_UP_DOWN
	CALL _write_vm_var
	LD DE, 0
	LD A, VM_VARIABLE_HERO_POS_JUMP_DOWN
	CALL _write_vm_var
	LD DE, 0
	LD A, VM_VARIABLE_HERO_POS_MASK
	CALL _write_vm_var
	LD DE, 0
	LD A, VM_VARIABLE_HERO_ACTION
	CALL _write_vm_var
	LD DE, 0
	LD A, VM_VARIABLE_HERO_ACTION_POS_MASK
	CALL _write_vm_var

	RET

	else ; TARGET_EXTENSION
	RET
	endif


CHECK_THREAD_REQUESTS:

	; Check if a part switch has been requested
	LD WA, (REQUESTED_NEXT_PART)
	CP WA, 0
	JP EQ, _no_part_switch

	; Validate part ID range before switching
	CP WA, GAME_PART_FIRST
	JP ULT, _invalid_part_switch
	CP WA, GAME_PART_LAST
	JP UGT, _invalid_part_switch

	; Part switch requested - call initForPart (WA = partId)
	CALL initForPart
_invalid_part_switch:
	LDW (REQUESTED_NEXT_PART), 0
_no_part_switch:

	LD A, 0
_check_thread_reqs__loop:

	; thread->state = thread->requested_state;
	; After applying, clear requested_state to NOT_FROZEN.
	; This matches the reference HLE where requested_state is a bool
	; and "= NO_REQUEST" (0xFFFF) truncates to true (UNFROZEN).
	; Effect: FREEZE is one-shot (lasts one frame, then auto-unfreezes).
	; This is critical for the death handler which FREEZEs all threads
	; then sets up threads 0 and 60 — without auto-unfreeze, they
	; stay frozen and the password display never runs.
	PUSH WA
	SLA 1, WA
	EXTZ XWA
	ADD XWA, VM_IS_CHANNEL_ACTIVE
	LD E, (XWA + REQUESTED_STATE)
	CP E, NO_STATE_REQUEST
	JP EQ, _no_state_request

I'm working on the Another World VM port for KN5000. The control panel serial communication has an issue: LEDs are turning on unexpectedly when we send serial commands to query button states.

The serial protocol works like this:
- We send a 2-byte command (cmd + param) to query a button segment
- Then send 2 dummy bytes (0xFF) to clock in the response
- The cpanel responds with [header][state]

The problem: those dummy 0xFF bytes are received BY THE CPANEL as a SECOND command. The cpanel's `process_command()` in MAME handles unrecognized commands (like 0xFF) by sending a sync packet [0x18][0x00]. But the sync packet response bytes are consumed by the NEXT query's first 2 exchanges — so the pipeline works.

However, the LED issue suggests byte alignment may be shifting. In the MAME cpanel code, LED commands are:
- Right panel: 0x00-0x04, 0x08, 0x0a-0x0c
- Left panel: 0xc0-0xc4, 0xc8

Our button query commands are:
- CPR_SEG4: cmd=0xE0, param=0x04
- CPL_SEG4: cmd=0x20, param=0x04

If byte alignment shifts by 1, the param byte 0x04 could be interpreted as the cmd byte of a new command. In the cpanel, cmd=0x04 IS a valid LED command!

Please read the MAME cpanel source code to understand:
1. What does cmd=0x04 do in process_command()? Is it an LED command?
2. What about cmd=0x20 — could it trigger LEDs?
3. What about cmd=0xE0?
4. Could the dummy 0xFF bytes cause LED activation?

Read the file: /home/fsanches/devel/kn5000-roms-disasm/mame_driver/src/devices/machine/kn5000_cpanel.cpp

Focus on `process_command()` and how commands are parsed. Look at the full command parsing logic.

## Analysis: MAME KN5000 CPPanel Serial Receive State Machine

Based on reading the MAME cpanel implementation, here's the detailed breakdown:

### 1. **How does the cpanel receive individual serial bytes?**

**Callback mechanism:** `void rxd(int state)` (line 117-120)
- This is called whenever the RXD line changes state
- Simply stores the bit value in `m_rxd` member variable
- Actual bit sampling happens on the **SIOCLK rising edge** in the `sioclk()` callback

**SIOCLK clock callback:** `void sioclk(int state)` (line 133-219)
- This drives the actual bit reception
- **Rising edge (state=1):** Lines 144-161
  - Samples the current RXD value: `m_rx_shift_register |= (m_rxd << 7)`
  - Shifts right to build up MSB-first: bits come in on bit 7, shift right
  - Decrements `m_rx_clock_count`
  - When count reaches 0, full byte is complete
- **Falling edge (state=0):** Lines 163-218 (handles TX output, not RX)

### 2. **How does it know when it has 2 bytes (cmd + param)?**

**Two-stage command assembly:**

**First byte received:** `process_received_byte()` (line 251-263)
- Stores byte in `m_cmd_buffer[m_cmd_index++]`
- With `m_cmd_index` starting at 0, first byte goes to `m_cmd_buffer[0]`

**Second byte received:**
- Goes to `m_cmd_buffer[1]`
- When `m_cmd_index >= 2`, line 257-261:
  ```c
  if (m_cmd_index >= 2) {
      process_command();
      m_cmd_index = 0;  // Reset for next 2-byte command
  }
  ```
- `process_command()` then interprets:
  - `m_cmd_buffer[0]` as **command** byte
  - `m_cmd_buffer[1]` as **parameter** byte

### 3. **What state is the byte counter in at startup?**

**device_reset()** (line 86-100):
```c
m_rx_clock_count = 8;     // Bits to receive (8 bits per byte)
m_tx_clock_count = 0;     // No TX in progress
m_cmd_index = 0;          // Waiting for byte 0 of command
```

**device_start()** (line 60-84):
- Constructor already initializes: `m_rx_clock_count(8)`, `m_cmd_index(0)` (line 40, 47)
- So the state is synchronized from the very start

### 4. **Is there any mechanism that could cause byte alignment to shift?**

**YES - The `tx_start()` callback (line 122-131):**
```c
void kn5000_cpanel_device::tx_start(int state)
{
    // Called when CPU starts transmitting a new byte - reset RX to sync byte boundaries
    if (state) {
        LOGMASKED(LOG_SERIAL, "cpanel tx_start: resetting RX counter for sync\n");
        m_rx_clock_count = 8;      // RESET to 8
        m_rx_shift_register = 0;   // CLEAR shift register
    }
}
```

**Critical insight:** 
- When the CPU starts transmitting (`tx_start(1)`), the cpanel **resets its RX state**
- This ensures **byte synchronization** - every CPU TX start signal realigns the RX byte boundary
- This prevents accumulated bit errors from causing misalignment
- Even if clock edges were missed, the next `tx_start()` call resets alignment

**No natural drift** - The RX counter only counts down by 1 per rising edge (line 150), never increments, and resets to 8 when a fresh byte completes. There's no mechanism for gradual drift.

### 5. **How do send_byte/send_button_packet/send_sync_packet work?**

**send_byte()** (line 221-249) - **Queuing mechanism:**

Three states:
1. **Immediate start** (if `m_tx_clock_count == 0` and no skip):
   - Sets `m_tx_shift_register = data`
   - Sets `m_tx_clock_count = 7` (7 bits left after pre-output)
   - **Pre-outputs bit 0 immediately** (line 233): `m_txd_cb(m_tx_shift_register & 1)`
   - Sets `m_tx_skip_first_falling` based on current clock state

2. **Queuing** (if TX is busy):
   - Pushes to `m_tx_queue` (line 246)
   - Waits for current byte to finish

3. **Chained bytes** (line 196-209):
   - When `m_tx_clock_count` reaches 0 and queue has more:
   - Loads next byte from queue: `m_tx_shift_register = m_tx_queue.front()`
   - Continues transmitting without resetting `m_tx_clock_count` (stays at pre-output state)

**send_sync_packet()** (line 355-360):
```c
void kn5000_cpanel_device::send_sync_packet()
{
    send_byte(0x18);   // Type 3 sync (bits 5-3 = 011)
    send_byte(0x00);   // Parameter
}
```
- Calls `send_byte()` twice
- First byte queued/starts immediately
- Second byte queued if first is still transmitting

**send_button_packet()** (line 375-401):
```c
send_byte(header);     // Packet header with segment & panel info
send_byte(state);      // Button state bitmap (8 bits per segment)
```
- Similarly queues two bytes
- Also calls `send_button_packet()` from `send_all_button_states()` which loops 11 times (line 403-410)
- This queues 22 bytes total (11 segments × 2 bytes each)

**Timer-driven TX clock** (line 560-569):
```c
TIMER_CALLBACK_MEMBER(kn5000_cpanel_device::timer_callback) {
    if (m_tx_clock_count > 0 || !m_tx_queue.empty()) {
        m_sclk_out_cb(1);  // Clock rising edge
        m_sclk_out_cb(0);  // Clock falling edge
    }
}
```
- Timer toggles the serial clock when there's data to send
- This drives the bit-shifting in the `sioclk()` callback

---

### Summary Table

| Question | Answer |
|----------|--------|
| Receive mechanism | `rxd()` callback stores bit; `sioclk()` callback on rising edge samples and shifts into `m_rx_shift_register` |
| 2-byte detection | `m_cmd_index` counter: increments on each byte received, triggers `process_command()` when >= 2 |
| Startup state | `m_rx_clock_count=8`, `m_cmd_index=0` (reset in `device_reset()`) |
| Alignment drift | `tx_start()` callback explicitly resets `m_rx_clock_count=8` and `m_rx_shift_register=0` when CPU begins TX |
| Send mechanism | `send_byte()` queues bytes; timer-driven `sioclk()` callback toggles clock to shift bits; chained bytes load from queue |

The **key safeguard** is `tx_start()` - it uses the CPU's transmission start signal to resynchronize the cpanel's RX byte boundary, ensuring the two devices stay aligned regardless of clock timing variations.

; _cpanel_init: Initialize control panel serial protocol
; Sends the 5-command init sequence matching the original firmware.
; Each command is followed by a delay. The cpanel MCUs respond with
; sync packets; we consume them via the standard 4-byte exchange.
; Must be called once before any _cpanel_query_segment calls.
; Clobbers: A, B, C, DE
_cpanel_init:
	; Init command 1: 1F DA
	LD B, 01Fh
	LD C, 0DAh
	CALL _cpanel_query_segment
	CALL _cpanel_delay

	; Init command 2: 1F 1A
	LD B, 01Fh
	LD C, 01Ah
	CALL _cpanel_query_segment
	CALL _cpanel_delay

	; Init command 3: 1D 00
	LD B, 01Dh
	LD C, 000h
	CALL _cpanel_query_segment
	CALL _cpanel_delay

	; Init command 4: DD 03
	LD B, 0DDh
	LD C, 003h
	CALL _cpanel_query_segment
	CALL _cpanel_delay

	; Init command 5: 1E 80
	LD B, 01Eh
	LD C, 080h
	CALL _cpanel_query_segment
	CALL _cpanel_delay

	; Clear serial interrupt flags (original firmware uses INTCLR)
	LD (INTCLR), 023h		; Clear INTTX1 pending
	LD (INTCLR), 022h		; Clear INTRX1 pending
	RET

; _cpanel_delay: Inter-command delay for init sequence
; Matches the original firmware's DELAY_3000_LOOPS between init commands.
; Clobbers: DE
_cpanel_delay:
	PUSH DE
	LD DE, 3000h
.loop:
	DJNZ DE, .loop
	POP DE
	RET

	endif ; TARGET_MAINCPU

INPUT_UPDATE_PLAYER:
	ifdef TARGET_MAINCPU

	; Query CPR_SEG4 (right panel segment 4) for direction buttons

VM_VARIABLE_HERO_POS_JUMP_DOWN	EQU 0FBh
VM_VARIABLE_HERO_POS_LEFT_RIGHT	EQU 0FCh
VM_VARIABLE_HERO_POS_MASK	EQU 0FDh
VM_VARIABLE_HERO_ACTION_POS_MASK EQU 0FEh
VM_VARIABLE_SCROLL_Y		EQU 0F9h

GAME_PART_FIRST			EQU 03E80h
GAME_PART_PROTECTION	EQU 03E80h	; Part 0: Copy protection
GAME_PART_INTRO			EQU 03E81h	; Part 1: Introduction cinematic
GAME_PART_WATER			EQU 03E82h	; Part 2: Water / lake

CALC_LINE_XMAX_AND_XMIN:
	; int16_t xmax = MAX(x1, x2);
	LD WA, (X1)
	CP WA, (X2)
	JP GT, XMAX_OK
	LD WA, (X2)
XMAX_OK:
	LD (LINE_XMAX), WA
	
	; int16_t xmin = MIN(x1, x2);
	LD WA, (X1)
	CP WA, (X2)
	JP LT, XMIN_OK
	LD WA, (X2)
XMIN_OK:
	LD (LINE_XMIN), WA
	RET

drawLineN:
	; Inputs:
	; C = color
	PUSH XIX
	PUSH XHL
	
	CALL CALC_LINE_XMAX_AND_XMIN

	; for (int16_t x=xmin; x<=xmax; x++)
	; 	m_curPagePtr1->pix(m_hliney, x) = color;
	LD XIX, (CUR_LINE)
	LD HL, (LINE_XMIN)
	EXTS XHL
	ADD XIX, XHL
	LD HL, (LINE_XMAX)
	SUB HL, (LINE_XMIN)
	INC HL				; inclusive range: xmax-xmin+1 pixels

drawLineN_loop:
	LDB (XIX), C
	INC XIX
	DJNZ HL, drawLineN_loop
	
	POP XHL
	POP XIX
	RET

drawLineP:
	; Copy pixels from PAGE_BITMAP_0 to curPagePtr1
	PUSH XIX
	PUSH XIY
	PUSH XHL

	CALL CALC_LINE_XMAX_AND_XMIN

	; Destination: CUR_LINE + LINE_XMIN (in curPagePtr1)
	LD XIX, (CUR_LINE)
	LD HL, (LINE_XMIN)
	EXTS XHL
	ADD XIX, XHL

	; Source: PAGE_BITMAP_0 + HLINEY*320 + LINE_XMIN
	LD XIY, PAGE_BITMAP_0
	LD XWA, 0
	LD WA, (HLINEY)
	LD DE, 320
	MUL XWA, DE
	ADD XIY, XWA
	LD XHL, 0
	LD HL, (LINE_XMIN)
	EXTS XHL
	ADD XIY, XHL

	; Loop: copy xmax-xmin+1 pixels
	LD HL, (LINE_XMAX)
	SUB HL, (LINE_XMIN)
	INC HL				; inclusive range: xmax-xmin+1 pixels

drawLineP_loop:
	LD C, (XIY)			; color = page_bitmap_0[y][x]
	LDB (XIX), C			; curPagePtr1[y][x] = color
	INC XIX
	INC XIY
	DJNZ HL, drawLineP_loop

	POP XHL
	POP XIY
	POP XIX
	RET

drawLineBlend:
	; Blend: read existing pixel, apply (color & 7) | 8
	PUSH XIX
	PUSH XHL

	CALL CALC_LINE_XMAX_AND_XMIN

	; curPagePtr1 scanline pointer
	LD XIX, (CUR_LINE)
	LD HL, (LINE_XMIN)
	EXTS XHL
	ADD XIX, XHL
	LD HL, (LINE_XMAX)
	SUB HL, (LINE_XMIN)
	INC HL				; inclusive range: xmax-xmin+1 pixels

drawLineBlend_loop:
	LD C, (XIX)			; color = curPagePtr1[y][x]
	ANDB C, 07h			; color &= 0x07
	ORB C, 08h			; color |= 0x08
	LDB (XIX), C			; curPagePtr1[y][x] = blended color
	INC XIX
	DJNZ HL, drawLineBlend_loop

	POP XHL
	POP XIX
	RET

drawPoint:

	PUSH DE				; save x
	LD XWA, 0
	LD WA, HL			; XWA = y (zero-extended 32-bit)
	LD DE, 320
	MUL XWA, DE			; XWA = y * 320
	POP DE				; restore x
	EXTZ XDE			; zero-extend x to 32-bit
	ADD XWA, XDE			; XWA = y*320 + x
	LD XIX, (CUR_PAGE_PTR_1)
	ADD XIX, XWA
	LDB (XIX), C			; write 1 byte (color)
	POP XIX
	RET

text MACRO stringid, x, y, color

	LD DE, x
	LD HL, y
	LD B, color

	CALL UPDATE_DISPLAY

	RET

	; A: PageID

	JP EQ, _UPDATE_DISPLAY

_UPDATE_DISPLAY_PAGEID_NOT_FE_OR_FF:

	LD XHL, (CUR_PAGE_PTR_2)
	LD XDE, 001a0000h + 20*320	; vga memory, skipping the first 20 lines because the image has 320x200 resolution and the screen has 320x240

	LD (CUR_PAGE_PTR_2), XIX

	SLA 2, IX
